extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers of The Spectator; readers interested in literature, theatre, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essays offering literary criticism (esp. epic/poetry), theatrical commentary (prologues/epilogues), and conduct/manners advice for a general educated readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of celebrated authors (but not servilely)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Critick... proposes to his Reader, that he should imitate the most celebrated Authors who have gone before him, and been engaged in Works of the same nature; as in particular, that if he writes on a poetical Subject, he should consider how Homer would have spoken on such an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One great Genius often catches the Flame from another, and writes in his Spirit, without copying servilely after him. Examples: many shining passages in Virgil lighted up by Homer; Milton raised and ennobled his Conceptions by such Imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and qualify scriptural/allusive material appropriate to the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton has numberless Allusions to glorious strokes of Poetry in Holy Writ... the great Critick... has taken notice of the sublime Manner in which the Lawgiver of the Jews has describ'd the Creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make use of such passages of Scripture as are proper to the poem, and duly qualify those high strains so they fit the poet's audience and subject (example: Milton selecting prophetic images but adapting their pitch for readers of 'colder Climates').

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of the sublime: portraying greatness either in tumult or calm
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sixth Book, like a troubled Ocean, represents Greatness in Confusion; the seventh Affects the Imagination like the Ocean in a Calm, and fills the Mind of the Reader, without producing in it any thing like Tumult or Agitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity may be achieved through violent, chaotic imagery or through vast, composed imagery — both can be sublime but produce different effects (tumult vs. serene elevation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ magnificent ideas and grand images to affect the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: They abound with as magnificent Ideas... The Poet has employ'd on them the whole Energy of our Tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large, elevated conceptions and high imaginative language (e.g., chariots of God, everlasting gates, golden compasses) to produce grandeur in description; such imagery should be coherent and vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloath abstract ideas in allegory and sensible images
rubrics_metrics.description: As Poetry delights in cloathing abstracted Ideas in Allegories and sensible Images, we find a magnificent Description of the Creation form'd after the same manner in one of the Prophets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating abstract or theological themes, embody them in concrete, sensible imagery or allegory to make them poetic and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate borrowing of classical/epic incidental devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thought of the Golden Compasses is conceived altogether in Homer's Spirit, and is a very noble Incident in this wonderful Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing characteristic epic devices (Homeric instruments, similes, conceits) is legitimate when they suit the subject and are reimagined rather than mechanically copied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential scenic construction and vivid particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The several great Scenes of the Creation rise up to view one after another, in such a manner, that the Reader seems present at this wonderful Work, and to assist among the Choirs of Angels, who are the Spectators of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange episodes and descriptive scenes so they proceed naturally and cumulatively, giving the reader the impression of witnessing events; use particulars to enliven vast subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise yet particular description of large subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: One would wonder how the Poet could be so concise in his Description of the six Days Works, as to comprehend them within the bounds of an Episode, and at the same time so particular, as to give us a lively Idea of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for economy of verse/description that nevertheless captures striking particulars — compress large actions into vivid episodic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue/Prologue as distinct performative pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one knows that on the British Stage they are distinct Performances by themselves, Pieces entirely detached from the Play, and no way essential to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat prologues/epilogues as independent entertainments; they may differ in tone from the main play without being improper simply for that reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue must arise from the occurrences of the play (be relevant)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the new Epilogue is written conformable to the Practice of our best Poets, so it is not such an one which... might serve for any other Play; but wholly rises out of the Occurrences of the Piece it was composed for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic epilogues; a good epilogue should be rooted in the events or characters of the play it follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tacking a comic tail to a tragic head when it breaks the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragi-Comedy... breaks the Tide of the Passions while they are yet flowing; ... tacking a Tragic Head with a Comic Tail, in order to refresh the Audience, is such a piece of Jargon, that I don't know what to make of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not undermine an ongoing tragic emotional arc by abruptly appending incongruous comedy; respect the integrity and emotional momentum of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider national/cultural stage-practices and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gaiety of it may be still the more proper, as it is at the end of a French Play; since every one knows that Nation... always close their Tragick Entertainments with what they call a Petite Piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging appropriateness of devices (e.g., a merry epilogue after tragedy), take into account cultural conventions and what the audience expects from that theatrical tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure theatrical success by audience reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Audience would not permit Mrs. Oldfield to go off the Stage the first Night, till she had repeated it twice... this has already been repeated nine times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular approval (calls for repetition, applause) is presented as evidence that an epilogue or performance succeeds with its contemporaneous audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness in a person: modest bearing and public virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the highest Instance of a noble Mind, to bear great Qualities without discovering in a Man's Behaviour any Consciousness that he is superior to the rest of the World... He ought to think no Man valuable but for his publick Spirit, Justice and Integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A truly great person conceals pride, values and exercises talents for public service, prizes justice and integrity over private display, and avoids ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentation and craving applause
rubrics_metrics.description: He who affects the Applauses and Addresses of a Multitude, or assumes to himself a Pre-eminence upon any other Consideration, must soon turn Admiration into Contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeking public adulation or assuming superiority for show undermines genuine esteem; virtues should be practiced without seeking fame for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female decency and primacy of domestic duties
rubrics_metrics.description: As Regard to Decency is a great Rule of Life in general, but more especially to be consulted by the Female World... The utmost of a Woman's Character is contained in Domestick Life; she is blameable or praiseworthy according as her Carriage affects the House of her Father or her Husband.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women should be judged primarily by conduct in domestic roles (daughter, sister, wife, mother), favour modest dress and behaviour over public ambition or conspicuousness, and avoid placing ambition on fleeting pleasures of youth and fortune.
